newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Hong Kong Mortgage Corp keeps funding options open.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong Mortgage Corp keeps funding options open.

text.p: Hong Kong's new Mortgage Corporation (HKMC) is getting set to launch mortgage-backed securities and unsecured debt later this year, but has yet to settle on how the issues will look, HKMC officials said.
The corporation has selected key executives and an office and is hiring 56 other staff.
But it has yet to settle on favoured investment instruments, maturities, issue sizes and currencies when it finally steps into the debt market and sells mortgage-backed securities.

"I would not confine it (mortgage corporation issues) to one single currency or one single product. We should be very flexible as long as it meets market demand," said Philip Li, manager of the corporation's debt issuance programme and treasury operations.
"I think we will look at all currencies, how they would swap back into Hong Kong dollars," said Leland Sun, who takes on the job of chief operating officer at the corporation on June 24.

Run by the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA), the corporation has the brief of easing Hong Kong banks' mismatch of funding between long-term lending and short-term borrowing and improving financing flows for home ownership.
Hong Kong's property market has ballooned in recent years, and some banks are nearing lending limits on home loans.
If nothing is done, the HKMA predicts a HK$788 billion gap between available mortgage funding and consumer demand by 2005.
The corporation will buy mortgages from banks, package them and then offer a mortgage-backed security (MBS) issue.
"It's a welcome avenue for banks to be able to originate mortgages and then shift them off (balance sheet)," said Jay Boice, head of new issues with BA Asia.
Sun said one of the corporation's first jobs would be issuing unsecured debt, while simultaneously accumulating mortgages on Hong Kong properties. An MBS would follow, he said.
The corporation was now embarking on a series of meetings to introduce itself and assess market mood, he said.
"We're not leaving any stone unturned as a new corporation," he said. "We're going to consult with the banking industry, consult with investment banks, commercial banks."
Both Li and Sun said it was too early to say whether corporation debt paper would enjoy automatic access to the HKMA's liquidity adjustment facility (LAF) or tax advantages.
LAF-eligible debt securities are more attractive to banks because they can be used as collateral to borrow cash. A profits tax exemption also would help issues' marketing value.
Boice said investors would want to know if there were any tax benefits, the level of government commitment, and what status the HKMA would afford the securities.
A HKMA official hinted that some advantages extended to other government-owned entities might be forthcoming.
"Draw your own conclusions -- in a corporation owned by the government," the official said.
Li did not expect strong competition from the private sector, but predicted that some mortgages that did not meet corporation criteria would be securitised privately.
Several local mortgage suppliers have recently launched MBS deals to clear their balance sheets.
Dah Sing Bank is issuing US$300 million in securitised mortgages this week, and Sanwa Bank's Hong Kong arm recently completed a US$144 million residential MBS.
Hong Kong Telecommunications Ltd also recently securitised a pool of staff mortgages.
